metadata.chapter_title: Similarity, Scale Factors, and Geometric Reasoning
metadata.title: Similar Triangles and Geometric Proofs
metadata.vcaa_description: Establish the conditions for similarity of triangles and use them to solve problems and prove geometric properties (including VC2M9SP01 angle properties).
metadata.target_mastery: Prove triangles are similar using AAA, SAS, SSS, and RHS similarity tests and calculate unknown side lengths in overlapping and non-overlapping triangles.
prerequisites: Parallel line and polygon angle properties (Year 8 VC2M8M05)

key_vocabulary.definition: Two geometric figures that have the exact same shape but not necessarily the same size; their corresponding angles are equal and their corresponding side lengths are in a constant ratio.
The constant ratio of any side length in the image (second figure) to the corresponding side length in the original (first figure): $k = \frac{\text{image length}}{\text{original length}}$.

Four minimum sufficient conditions to prove two triangles are similar: Angle-Angle-Angle ($\text{AAA}$), Side-Angle-Side ($\text{SAS}$ in ratio), Side-Side-Side ($\text{SSS}$ in ratio), and Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side ($\text{RHS}$ in ratio).
Pairs of sides located opposite equal angles in two similar triangles, whose lengths form equal ratios.

theory.title: The Four Similarity Tests for Triangles (AAA, SAS, SSS, RHS)
theory.explanation: Two triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$ are similar (written $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$, with vertices listed in matching order) if they satisfy any one of four tests: (1) $\text{AAA}$ (or $\text{AA}$): two pairs of corresponding angles are equal (the third pair is automatically equal by the $180^\circ$ angle sum); (2) $\text{SAS}$: two pairs of corresponding sides are in the same ratio and the included angles between them are equal; (3) $\text{SSS}$: all three pairs of corresponding sides are in the same constant ratio $k$; (4) $\text{RHS}$: both triangles contain a $90^\circ$ right angle, and the hypotenuses and one pair of shorter sides are in the same ratio.
theory.formula_latex: \triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF \iff \frac{DE}{AB} = \frac{EF}{BC} = \frac{DF}{AC} = k \quad \text{and} \quad \angle A = \angle D,\; \angle B = \angle E,\; \angle C = \angle F
theory.callout_title: Vertex Order Locks In the Side Ratios
theory.callout_rule: Once you write $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ in matching angle order, the corresponding side ratios can be read straight from the letters without even looking at the diagram: $\frac{DE}{AB} = \frac{EF}{BC} = \frac{DF}{AC}$.

theory.title: Finding Unknown Side Lengths Using Scale Factors and Proportions
theory.explanation: Once two triangles are known or proved to be similar, any unknown side length can be found either by calculating the scale factor $k = \frac{\text{image}}{\text{original}}$ from a known pair of corresponding sides, or by setting up a proportion equation with the unknown in the numerator. Always match sides that lie opposite equal angles.
theory.callout_title: Put the Unknown Side on Top
theory.callout_rule: When writing a similarity proportion, always place the unknown pronumeral $x$ in the numerator on the left-hand side so that solving takes just one multiplication step.

theory.title: Overlapping and Parallel-Line Triangles in Geometric Proofs
theory.explanation: When a line segment $DE$ is drawn parallel to the base $BC$ of $\triangle ABC$ (with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$), the smaller triangle $\triangle ADE$ and the full triangle $\triangle ABC$ share a common angle at $A$, and have equal corresponding angles $\angle ADE = \angle ABC$ and $\angle AED = \angle ACB$ on the parallel lines. Therefore $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$ by $\text{AAA}$. Similarly, a bowtie (hourglass) configuration formed by parallel lines creates similar triangles via vertically opposite angles and alternate angles.
theory.callout_title: Use Full Side Lengths in Nested Triangles
theory.callout_rule: In a nested triangle $\triangle ADE$ inside $\triangle ABC$, the side of the large triangle is the FULL length $AB = AD + DB$, never just the lower piece $DB$ when comparing with the parallel bases $DE$ and $BC$.

worked_examples.title: Proving Two Triangles Are Similar and Finding a Scale Factor
worked_examples.problem: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 6\text{ cm}$, $BC = 9\text{ cm}$, and $\angle ABC = 52^\circ$. In $\triangle PQR$, $PQ = 10\text{ cm}$, $QR = 15\text{ cm}$, and $\angle PQR = 52^\circ$. (a) Write a formal similarity proof to show that $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$. (b) If $AC = 7.2\text{ cm}$, find the length of $PR$.

steps.thinking: Calculate the ratios of the two pairs of given sides around the $52^\circ$ included angle.
State the equal included angles and conclude similarity with the correct test and vertex order.
steps.working:
$$\angle ABC = \angle PQR = 52^\circ \text{ (given included angle)}$$
$$\therefore \triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR \; (\text{SAS similarity},\; k = \tfrac{5}{3})$$

steps.thinking: Multiply $AC = 7.2\text{ cm}$ by the linear scale factor $k = \frac{5}{3}$ to find $PR$.

now_you_try.problem: Triangle $DEF$ has side lengths $4\text{ cm}$, $7\text{ cm}$, and $9\text{ cm}$. Triangle $XYZ$ has side lengths $10\text{ cm}$, $17.5\text{ cm}$, and $22.5\text{ cm}$. State the similarity test that proves $\triangle DEF \sim \triangle XYZ$ and find the scale factor $k$.
now_you_try.hint: Check whether $\frac{10}{4}$, $\frac{17.5}{7}$, and $\frac{22.5}{9}$ simplify to the same number.
now_you_try.working_summary: $\frac{10}{4} = 2.5$, $\frac{17.5}{7} = 2.5$, and $\frac{22.5}{9} = 2.5$, so $\triangle DEF \sim \triangle XYZ$ by $\text{SSS}$ with $k = 2.5$ (or $\frac{5}{2}$).

worked_examples.title: Finding Unknown Lengths in Overlapping Parallel-Line Triangles
worked_examples.problem: In $\triangle ABC$, point $D$ lies on $AB$ and point $E$ lies on $AC$ such that $DE \parallel BC$. Given $AD = 8\text{ cm}$, $DB = 4\text{ cm}$, and $DE = 10\text{ cm}$, prove that $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$ and calculate the length of the base $BC$.

steps.thinking: Prove $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$ using the common angle at $A$ and corresponding angles on parallel lines $DE \parallel BC$.
steps.working:
$$\angle DAE = \angle BAC \text{ (common angle)}$$
$$\angle ADE = \angle ABC \text{ (corresponding angles, } DE \parallel BC\text{)}$$
$$\therefore \triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC \; (\text{AAA})$$

steps.thinking: Find the full side length $AB = AD + DB = 8 + 4 = 12\text{ cm}$ and equate ratios of corresponding sides.

now_you_try.problem: In $\triangle PQR$, $ST \parallel QR$ with $S$ on $PQ$ and $T$ on $PR$. If $PS = 6\text{ cm}$, $SQ = 9\text{ cm}$, and $QR = 20\text{ cm}$, find the length of $ST$.
now_you_try.hint: The full side is $PQ = 6 + 9 = 15\text{ cm}$, and $\frac{ST}{QR} = \frac{PS}{PQ}$.
now_you_try.working_summary: $PQ = 15\text{ cm}$. Since $\triangle PST \sim \triangle PQR$ ($\text{AAA}$), $\frac{ST}{20} = \frac{6}{15} \implies ST = 20 \times \frac{2}{5} = 8\text{ cm}$.

worked_examples.title: Indirect Shadow Measurement Using Similar Right-Angled Triangles
worked_examples.problem: In Melbourne's Royal Botanic Gardens, a vertical $1.8\text{ m}$ sighting pole casts a horizontal shadow of length $2.4\text{ m}$ at the same instant that a tall eucalyptus tree casts a horizontal shadow of length $18\text{ m}$. Assuming the sun's rays are parallel, calculate the height $h$ of the eucalyptus tree.

steps.thinking: Both the pole and the tree stand vertically ($90^\circ$ to the horizontal ground), and the parallel sun rays meet the ground at equal angles, so the two right-angled shadow triangles are similar by $\text{AAA}$.
Multiply both sides by $1.8$ to solve for $h$.

now_you_try.problem: A $1.5\text{ m}$ fence post casts a $2.0\text{ m}$ shadow at the same time a stadium light tower casts a $36\text{ m}$ shadow. How tall is the light tower?

common_misconceptions.title: Using the Partial Segment Instead of the Full Side in Nested Triangles
common_misconceptions.misconception: When $DE \parallel BC$ inside $\triangle ABC$, students often write $\frac{DE}{BC} = \frac{AD}{DB}$ using the lower side segment $DB$ instead of the full triangle side $AB = AD + DB$.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: Because $BC$ is a side of the complete triangle $\triangle ABC$, its ratio partner must be the complete side $AB = AD + DB$ of $\triangle ABC$. The trapezoid segment $DB$ is not a side of any triangle.
common_misconceptions.incorrect_working: $$AD = 6,\; DB = 3,\; DE = 8: \quad \frac{8}{BC} = \frac{6}{3} \implies BC = 4 \quad \text{(Incorrect — smaller than } DE\text{!)}$$
common_misconceptions.counter_example: If $AD = 6$ and $DB = 3$, the base $BC$ is clearly wider than $DE = 8$; using $\frac{6}{3}$ wrongly makes $BC = 4$.

common_misconceptions.title: Applying SAS Similarity When the Equal Angle Is Not Included
common_misconceptions.misconception: Concluding two triangles are similar by $\text{SAS}$ when two sides are in ratio and a non-included angle is equal.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: For $\text{SAS}$ similarity, the equal angle MUST be the included angle sandwiched directly between the two proportional sides.
common_misconceptions.incorrect_working: $$\frac{AB}{DE} = \frac{BC}{EF} \text{ and } \angle A = \angle D \implies \triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF \text{ by SAS} \quad \text{(Incorrect)}$$
common_misconceptions.correct_working: $$\frac{AB}{DE} = \frac{BC}{EF} \text{ requires the included angle } \angle B = \angle E \text{ for SAS similarity.}$$
common_misconceptions.counter_example: Just like the ambiguous case in congruence, two side lengths and a non-included acute angle can form two completely different non-similar triangles.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Given that $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ with $AB = 5\text{ cm}$, $BC = 8\text{ cm}$, $DE = 15\text{ cm}$, and $EF = x\text{ cm}$, find the linear scale factor $k$ and the value of $x$.
step_by_step_solution: Calculate the linear scale factor from the corresponding sides $AB$ and $DE$: $k = \frac{DE}{AB} = \frac{15}{5} = 3$.
Multiply $BC = 8\text{ cm}$ by $k = 3$: $x = 3 \times 8 = 24$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Determine whether $\triangle ABC$ with sides $6\text{ cm}, 8\text{ cm}, 12\text{ cm}$ and $\triangle DEF$ with sides $9\text{ cm}, 12\text{ cm}, 18\text{ cm}$ are similar. If so, state the similarity test and scale factor $k$.
step_by_step_solution: Match shortest, middle, and longest sides: $\frac{9}{6} = 1.5$, $\frac{12}{8} = 1.5$, and $\frac{18}{12} = 1.5$.
Since all three pairs of corresponding sides are in the same ratio $k = 1.5$, $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ by $\text{SSS}$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Two right-angled triangles $\triangle ABC$ ($\angle B = 90^\circ$) and $\triangle DEF$ ($\angle E = 90^\circ$) have hypotenuses $AC = 10\text{ cm}$ and $DF = 25\text{ cm}$, and shorter sides $AB = 6\text{ cm}$ and $DE = 15\text{ cm}$. State the similarity test that proves $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ and find $EF$ if $BC = 8\text{ cm}$.
step_by_step_solution: Check the ratio of the hypotenuses and shorter legs: $\frac{DF}{AC} = \frac{25}{10} = 2.5$ and $\frac{DE}{AB} = \frac{15}{6} = 2.5$ with $\angle B = \angle E = 90^\circ$, so $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ by $\text{RHS}$.
Multiply $BC = 8\text{ cm}$ by $k = 2.5$: $EF = 8 \times 2.5 = 20\text{ cm}$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: In $\triangle ABC$, a line $DE$ is parallel to $BC$ with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$. If $AD = 9\text{ cm}$, $DB = 6\text{ cm}$, and $BC = 20\text{ cm}$, find the length of $DE$.
step_by_step_solution: By $\text{AAA}$ similarity, $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$, where the full side is $AB = 9 + 6 = 15\text{ cm}$.
Set up $\frac{DE}{20} = \frac{9}{15} = \frac{3}{5} \implies DE = 20 \times \frac{3}{5} = 12\text{ cm}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: Two straight segments $AB$ and $CD$ intersect at point $X$ between parallel riverbanks $AC \parallel BD$ along the Yarra River. A surveyor measures $AX = 12\text{ m}$, $BX = 30\text{ m}$, and the bank baseline $AC = 18\text{ m}$. Find the width $BD$ on the opposite bank.
step_by_step_solution: Since $AC \parallel BD$, alternate angles $\angle XAC = \angle XBD$ and vertically opposite angles $\angle AXC = \angle BXD$ are equal, so $\triangle AXC \sim \triangle BXD$ ($\text{AAA}$).
Equate corresponding sides: $\frac{BD}{AC} = \frac{BX}{AX} \implies \frac{BD}{18} = \frac{30}{12} = 2.5 \implies BD = 45\text{ m}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: An A-frame ski chalet roof at Mount Buller has rafters of total length $7.5\text{ m}$ from the apex $A$ to the eaves $B$ and $C$, where the ground floor width is $BC = 9.0\text{ m}$. A horizontal ceiling joist $DE$ is installed $5.0\text{ m}$ down the rafters from the apex $A$. Find the width of the ceiling joist $DE$.
step_by_step_solution: Since $DE \parallel BC$, $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$ ($\text{AAA}$) with $AD = 5.0\text{ m}$ and $AB = 7.5\text{ m}$.
Solve $\frac{DE}{9.0} = \frac{5.0}{7.5} = \frac{2}{3} \implies DE = 6.0\text{ m}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A student places a small flat mirror horizontally on the ground $3\text{ m}$ from the base of a flagpole and steps back $1.2\text{ m}$ from the mirror until she sees the top of the flagpole centred in the mirror. If her eyes are $1.6\text{ m}$ above the ground, and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, how tall is the flagpole?
step_by_step_solution: Both the student and flagpole are vertical ($90^\circ$) and the reflection angles at the mirror are equal, so the two right-angled triangles are similar by $\text{AAA}$.
Solve $\frac{h}{1.6} = \frac{3}{1.2} = 2.5 \implies h = 4\text{ m}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A ramp rises uniformly from ground level to a loading dock. At a horizontal distance of $2.4\text{ m}$ from the start of the ramp, a vertical support strut of height $0.45\text{ m}$ touches the underside of the ramp. If the total horizontal length of the ramp is $6.4\text{ m}$, find the height of the loading dock.
step_by_step_solution: The vertical strut and the vertical loading dock form similar right-angled triangles with the horizontal ground ($\text{AAA}$).
Solve $\frac{H}{0.45} = \frac{6.4}{2.4} = \frac{8}{3} \implies H = 0.45 \times \frac{8}{3} = 1.2\text{ m}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$ with $AD = x\text{ cm}$, $DB = 5\text{ cm}$, $AE = 6\text{ cm}$, and $EC = 7.5\text{ cm}$. Prove that $\frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{AE}{AC}$ and hence solve for $x$.
step_by_step_solution: Since $DE \parallel BC$, $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$ ($\text{AAA}$), so $\frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{AE}{AC}$ where $AB = x + 5$ and $AC = 6 + 7.5 = 13.5$.
Solve $\frac{x}{x + 5} = \frac{6}{13.5} = \frac{4}{9} \implies 9x = 4x + 20 \implies 5x = 20 \implies x = 4$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Explain why all equilateral triangles are similar to one another, whereas not all isosceles triangles are similar.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: Every equilateral triangle has angles $60^\circ, 60^\circ, 60^\circ$ ($\text{AAA}$), whereas isosceles triangles can have different apex angles (e.g. $40^\circ, 70^\circ, 70^\circ$ vs $100^\circ, 40^\circ, 40^\circ$)
step_by_step_solution: Every equilateral triangle has all three interior angles equal to $60^\circ$, so any two equilateral triangles satisfy the $\text{AAA}$ similarity test.
Two isosceles triangles can have completely different interior angles (such as $40^\circ, 70^\circ, 70^\circ$ and $100^\circ, 40^\circ, 40^\circ$), failing $\text{AAA}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: In a right-angled triangle $\triangle ABC$ with $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$, an altitude $BD$ is drawn perpendicular to the hypotenuse $AC$. Prove that $\triangle ADB \sim \triangle BDC$ and deduce that $BD^2 = AD \times DC$. If $AD = 4\text{ cm}$ and $DC = 9\text{ cm}$, find $BD$.
step_by_step_solution: Let $\angle DAB = \theta$. Then in right-angled $\triangle ADB$, $\angle ABD = 90^\circ - \theta$. Since $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$, $\angle DBC = 90^\circ - (90^\circ - \theta) = \theta = \angle DAB$. With $\angle ADB = \angle BDC = 90^\circ$, $\triangle ADB \sim \triangle BDC$ ($\text{AAA}$).
Equating corresponding sides gives $\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{AD}{BD} \implies BD^2 = AD \times DC = 4 \times 9 = 36 \implies BD = 6\text{ cm}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Two vertical poles of heights $a = 3\text{ m}$ and $b = 6\text{ m}$ stand on horizontal ground. Taut wires connect the top of each pole to the base of the other pole, crossing at height $h$ above the ground. Using similar triangles, show that $\frac{1}{h} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$ regardless of the distance between the poles, and calculate $h$.
step_by_step_solution: Let the horizontal distance between the poles be $d$, divided into $d_1 + d_2 = d$ at the point directly below the intersection. By similar right-angled triangles, $\frac{h}{a} = \frac{d_2}{d}$ and $\frac{h}{b} = \frac{d_1}{d}$.
Adding the two equations gives $\frac{h}{a} + \frac{h}{b} = \frac{d_1 + d_2}{d} = 1 \implies \frac{1}{h} = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{2} \implies h = 2\text{ m}$.
